html:
The Muisca were the people of the high plateau around Bogotá and Tunja in the Eastern Andes of Colombia, before and after the Spanish conquest. They spoke Chibcha and were one of the great farming peoples of the Americas, with potatoes, maize and quinoa on the cool plateau.

When the Spanish came they were split into two main chiefdoms: the zipa ruled the south from Bacatá, near Bogotá, and the zaque ruled the north from Hunza, today Tunja. They traded salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón, emeralds and cotton cloth with the lowlands for gold, which their smiths cast into fine offerings.

A rite at Lake Guatavita, where a new chief covered in gold dust washed in the lake while gold was thrown into it, fed the Spanish legend of El Dorado. Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada reached the plateau in 1537 and took it within a year; Santa Fe de Bogotá was founded in 1538 as part of Spanish America. The Muisca language faded by the 1700s, but many Colombians descend from them. The gold Muisca raft, found in 1969, is in the Gold Museum in Bogotá.
